newsitem.title: JAPAN: Media links Japan lawmakers to arrested oil trader.
newsitem.headline: Media links Japan lawmakers to arrested oil trader.

text.p: An obscure Japanese tax evasion case has taken on political overtones with a growing number of news reports saying that a Japanese oil dealer now in custody made donations to some of the nation's key politicians.
The revelations could be an embarrassment for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new minority government formed only last week.

Quoting unidentified sources, Kyodo news agency said on Monday that a "powerful" incumbent Lower House legislator had received several million yen (tens of thousands of U.S. dollars) from millionaire oil wholesaler Junichi Izui.
The politician, whose name was withheld, did not report the donation in his tax return as required, Kyodo said.
Japanese newspapers have also reported that Izui had ties to political figures, making donations and purchasing tickets to fund-raising events.
Izui, owner and sole employee of oil wholesaler Izui Oil Co, was arrested last Thursday on charges he evaded 310 million yen ($2.80 million) in taxes.

Izui handed over to the authorities a notebook in which he had recorded banquet dates and the names of 16 politicians, Kyodo said. Also written in the notebook were the names of "many" bureaucrats from ministries including the powerful Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), it said.
Investigators and government officials declined to comment on the report and calls to Izui's office in Osaka went unanswered.
The scandal involves a series of complicated deals involving Izui and oil giants Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Mitsui Mining Co.

In a separate report at the weekend, Kyodo quoted company sources as saying that when Izui proposed a deal to Mitsui Mining last year, he mentioned the names of several officials at MITI and the Natural Resources and Energy Agency.

Kyodo says the Osaka oil dealer wined and dined MITI officials and made legal political donations to at least five lawmakers, including Taku Yamasaki, the policy chief of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).

In a news conference on Thursday after the first meeting of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new cabinet, new Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said he met Izui two or three times at fund-raising parties.
"I believe I have not done anything illegal," he said.

LDP secretary-general Koichi Kato also said he met Izui at a private function a few years ago. Izui bought 200,000 yen ($1,800) worth of fund-raising party tickets, Kyodo said. But Kato denied having any specific relationship with him, Kyodo said.
Japan has been rocked by a series of scandals and controversies involving overly cosy or improper links between government officials and businessmen.
In one such case last year, then Finance Minister Masayoshi Takemura docked his own pay over a scandal involving a senior ministry official taking improper gifts from business contacts.

One of the biggest political scandals of recent years was the 1980s Recruit stocks-for-favours affair that was seen as a symbol of the excesses of the nation's "bubble economy" era of inflated land and share prices.

Many of Japan's senior politicians, bureaucrats and business executives were believed to have received shares of Tokyo-based job information company Recruit Cosmos before the stock was listed and its price jumped. The scandal caused a bitter political furore that led to the downfall of Prime Minister Noboru Takeshita in June 1989. ($1=111 yen)
